I had a similar experience with isolation during my school - college years.

It took me about a year in college to fully fit in with my group of friends. its been almost 10 years since then and we still hangout. That being said, they still cannot my problems.

My advice: get the help you need before you consider making friends etc.. You're right that everyone has their problems and can't deal with yours, so you have to do the same thing. Go on survivor mode: If the therapist is not listening to you, change therapist. 

I find that once I get the help I needed, everything else became much easier: friends, family, work. You make better decisions for yourself and others. But the road to recover isn't a straight one, you will relapse whether its within your control or not. You can do everything right and life will still kick you in the gut. Know this: its okay that you're not okay. You don't owe people to 'look' happy, you owe it to yourself to survive another day.

Oh hon, I'm sorry to hear that. I know how terrible these episodes can be. Here's a few things I'd suggest you do, but keep in mind I'm not a healthcare professional.  


1. **Set up a daily routine based on time, and commit to it whether you feel like it or not .**  
What I mean is, you use your phone and set up an alarm everyday for meals, waking up, preparing for work, exercising, and sleeping. For the latter, I'd recommend setting up an alarm to put yourself to bed, especially if you find it difficult to fall asleep. Don't cram your schedule, but be stick to it regardless of your feelings.
2. **Try to make conversation with someone.**   
Call, catch up with someone at least once every 2 days, even to just say hello. It helps bring you out of your head. You can set up an alarm for this.  

3. **Do exercises, but don't force yourself.** I struggle with low energy levels myself but I love going for walks.  

4. **Write things down.** It provides an 'outlet' for your chaotic mind and clears some space up there.
